concepts.name: Indices and exponential equations
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (assumed knowledge for Cambridge 0606, where it is used but not tested directly). What an index is; the laws of indices including zero, negative and rational (fractional) indices; simplifying numerical and algebraic expressions with indices without a calculator; and exponential equations solved by writing both sides as powers of the same base (for example 4^(x+1) = 8^x) or by a substitution that gives a quadratic in a^x (for example 2^(2x) − 6 × 2^x + 8 = 0). Equations that need logarithms are in amath.logs.equations.

concepts.name: Surds
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (assumed knowledge for Cambridge 0606, where exact answers often need surds). Rational and irrational numbers, simplifying surds (√50 = 5√2), adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing surds, expanding brackets containing surds, rationalising denominators of the forms a√b and a ± √b, and giving exact answers in simplest surd form.

concepts.name: Polynomials: terms, operations and division
concepts.description: What a polynomial is (terms, degree, coefficients, leading term, constant term); adding, subtracting and multiplying polynomials (ZIMSEC: order not more than three); algebraic long division of a polynomial by a linear expression ax + b, giving the quotient and remainder; and the identity dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder. Finding the quadratic factor of a cubic by division or by comparing coefficients is practised in amath.polynomials.cubic-equations.

concepts.name: The remainder and factor theorems
concepts.description: The remainder theorem (the remainder on dividing f(x) by x − a is f(a); by ax + b it is f(−b/a)) and the factor theorem (x − a is a factor when f(a) = 0); testing whether an expression is a factor; finding unknown coefficients from a given factor or remainder, including two unknowns from two conditions (simultaneous equations).

concepts.name: Factorising cubics and solving cubic equations
concepts.description: Finding a first linear factor of a cubic by trying factors of the constant term with the factor theorem, finding the quadratic factor by long division, comparing coefficients or inspection, factorising completely, and solving cubic equations (including the case where the quadratic factor gives surd roots by the formula); checking roots by substitution. Sketching cubics is in amath.graphs.cubic.

concepts.name: Identities and unknown coefficients
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The difference between an identity (≡, true for every value of the variable) and an equation; finding unknown coefficients in an identity by equating coefficients of like powers or by substituting convenient values (for example writing 2x² + 12x + 13 ≡ a(x + b)² + c, or x³ − 2x² + 4 ≡ (x − 1)(Ax² + Bx + C) + R).

concepts.name: Linear inequalities
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Solving linear inequalities in one variable, including double inequalities and reversing the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number; showing solution sets on a number line and in set notation; listing integer solutions. Quadratic inequalities are in amath.quadratics.inequalities; modulus inequalities (Cambridge) are in amath.modulus.inequalities.

concepts.name: Simultaneous equations: one linear and one non-linear
concepts.description: Solving a pair of simultaneous equations in two unknowns where one is linear and the other quadratic or otherwise non-linear (for example x² − 3xy + y² + 19 = 0, xy = 3, or x/y + 2y/x = 4) by substitution or elimination, pairing the solutions correctly, and interpreting the solutions as the intersection points of a line and a curve. Two linear equations are assumed knowledge and only revised briefly.

concepts.name: Equations reducible to quadratic form
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Recognising and making the substitution that turns an equation into a quadratic (u = x^(1/3), u = √x, u = ln x, u = eˣ, u = 2ˣ), solving the quadratic, substituting back and rejecting impossible values (eˣ > 0, √x ≥ 0), with exact and 3-significant-figure answers.

concepts.name: Solving quadratic equations
concepts.description: Solving quadratic equations for real roots by factorising, by completing the square and by the quadratic formula (exact surd answers and answers to 3 significant figures), rearranging equations into the form ax² + bx + c = 0 first, forming and solving quadratic equations from problems, and checking answers.

concepts.name: Completing the square, maximum and minimum values and quadratic graphs
concepts.description: Writing ax² + bx + c in the form a(x + p)² + q; reading off the vertex (turning point), the line of symmetry and the maximum or minimum value; sketching y = f(x) with its intercepts and vertex; finding the range of a quadratic function for a given domain with correct notation; the quadratic as a two-to-one (many-one) mapping. The maximum or minimum by differentiation is mentioned and links to amath.calculus.stationary-points.

concepts.name: The discriminant and the nature of roots
concepts.description: The discriminant b² − 4ac and the conditions for two distinct real roots, two equal roots or no real roots; finding the values or range of a constant k for which an equation has equal, real or no real roots; and (Cambridge depth) the related conditions for a given line to intersect a curve at two points, to be a tangent to it, or not to meet it, by forming a quadratic and using its discriminant.

concepts.name: Quadratic inequalities
concepts.description: Solving quadratic inequalities (>, <, ≥, ≤) by finding the critical values and using a sketch of the parabola or a sign table, writing solution sets in the correct form (−3 < x < 4; x < 1 or x > 6), and inequalities that arise from discriminant conditions (the range of k for which a line meets a curve).

concepts.name: Modulus equations
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The meaning of |x| as the non-negative value; solving |ax + b| = c, |ax + b| = cx + d (checking each solution), |ax + b| = |cx + d| (by squaring or by cases) and |ax² + bx + c| = d, algebraically and with graphs.

concepts.name: Modulus inequalities
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Solving k|ax + b| > c, k|ax + b| ≤ c, k|ax + b| ≤ |cx + d|, |ax + b| ≤ cx + d, |ax² + bx + c| > d and |ax² + bx + c| ≤ d graphically or algebraically (critical values, squaring both sides when both are non-negative), and writing the solution set correctly.

concepts.name: Graphs of y = |f(x)|
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The relationship between y = f(x) and y = |f(x)| (the parts below the x-axis are reflected in it, giving cusps) for linear, quadratic and trigonometric functions (y = a sin bx + c, a cos bx + c, a tan bx + c), intercepts and key points, and using the graphs to find the number of solutions of equations such as |f(x)| = k. Moduli of cubics are in amath.graphs.cubic.

concepts.name: Cubic graphs and cubic inequalities
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Sketching cubic graphs given as a product of three linear factors (intercepts labelled, shape for a positive or negative leading coefficient, a repeated factor touching the axis), sketching the modulus of such a cubic, and solving cubic inequalities of the form f(x) ≥ d, > d, ≤ d, < d graphically, where f(x) is a product of three linear factors.

concepts.name: Functions: mappings, domain and range
concepts.description: Mappings and functions (explaining in words why a relation is or is not a function), one-one and many-one functions, function notation f(x) and f : x ↦ …, domain and range (image set), finding the range of linear, quadratic, exponential and logarithmic functions over a given domain, restricting a domain, and illustrating functions with graphs.

concepts.name: Composite functions
concepts.description: Forming composite functions fg(x) = f(g(x)) and f²(x) = f(f(x)), the fact that fg and gf usually differ, the domain and range of a composite (the range of g must lie in the domain of f), evaluating composites and solving equations such as fg(x) = 5.

concepts.name: Inverse functions
concepts.description: When a function has an inverse (it must be one-one), explaining in words why a function has no inverse and restricting its domain so that it has one, finding f⁻¹(x) algebraically with correct notation (including quadratic, exponential and logarithmic functions), the domain and range of f⁻¹, ff⁻¹(x) = x, and sketching a function and its inverse as reflections in the line y = x.

concepts.name: Logarithms and the laws of logarithms
concepts.description: The definition log_a b = c ⇔ a^c = b, converting between index and logarithmic form, common logarithms (lg) and natural logarithms (ln, base e), the laws of logarithms (product, quotient, power, log_a a = 1, log_a 1 = 0), change of base, writing expressions as a single logarithm and evaluating logarithms without a calculator.

concepts.name: Exponential and logarithmic equations
concepts.description: Solving equations of the form a^x = b with logarithms (exact form and 3 significant figures), equations with different bases (for example 2^(x+1) = 3^x), logarithmic equations using the laws (for example log₂(x + 1) − log₂ x = 3) with a check that every logarithm is defined, equations involving e and ln, and simple exponential growth and decay problems. Equations that become quadratics in eˣ or ln x are in amath.algebra.substitution.

concepts.name: Graphs of exponential and logarithmic functions
concepts.description: The shapes and key features of y = eˣ, y = ln x, y = aˣ and y = log_a x, and of y = ke^(nx) + a and y = k ln(ax + b) (n, k, a, b integers): intercepts, asymptotes and their equations, growth and decay; eˣ and ln x as inverse functions (reflection in y = x); sketching a logarithmic graph and its inverse (ZIMSEC).

concepts.name: Straight lines: distance, midpoint, gradient and equation
concepts.description: The distance between two points, the midpoint of a line segment, gradient, the equation of a straight line in the forms y = mx + c, y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and ax + by + c = 0, intercepts, the intersection of two lines, collinear points and areas of triangles and quadrilaterals with given vertices.

concepts.name: Parallel and perpendicular lines
concepts.description: The conditions m₁ = m₂ for parallel lines and m₁m₂ = −1 for perpendicular lines, equations of lines parallel or perpendicular to a given line through a point, the normal to a line, the perpendicular bisector of a line segment, the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line, and problems with triangles and quadrilaterals (right angles, kites, rhombuses).

concepts.name: Reducing relationships to straight-line form
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Transforming a relationship to the straight-line form Y = mX + c (for example y = Axⁿ to lg y = n lg x + lg A, y = Abˣ to lg y = x lg b + lg A, y = A/x + B), finding the unknown constants from the gradient and intercept of the transformed line, and converting a given straight line (for example of y² against x³, or of e^(2y) against x²) back into an equation in x and y.

concepts.name: The equation of a circle
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r² of a circle with centre (a, b) and radius r, the expanded form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, finding the centre and radius by completing the square, finding the equation from a centre and a point or from the ends of a diameter, and deciding whether a point is inside, on or outside a circle.

concepts.name: Circles, lines and tangents
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Finding the points where a line meets a circle, deciding whether a line is a tangent, a chord or does not meet the circle (discriminant, or the distance from the centre compared with the radius), the equation of the tangent at a point (perpendicular to the radius) and other tangent problems, without calculus.

concepts.name: Intersecting circles
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Deciding whether two circles intersect, touch (externally or internally) or do not meet by comparing the distance between the centres with r₁ + r₂ and |r₁ − r₂|, finding the points of intersection, and finding the equation of the common chord by subtracting the equations.

concepts.name: Radian measure, arc length and sector area
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The radian, converting between degrees and radians, exact radian values (π/6, π/4, π/3, …), arc length s = rθ and sector area A = ½r²θ with θ in radians (formulas not given in the exam), the perimeter of a sector, and finding r or θ from given information.

concepts.name: Arcs, sectors and segments in compound shapes
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Chord lengths and segment areas (½r²(θ − sin θ)), perimeters and areas of compound shapes made of sectors, segments, triangles and rectangles, using right-angled trigonometry and the sine and cosine rules (given in the List of formulas) with radian measure; exact answers in terms of π and surds where asked.

concepts.name: The six trigonometric functions of any angle
concepts.description: Sine, cosine and tangent and their reciprocals secant, cosecant and cotangent; definitions for angles of any size in degrees or radians (the four quadrants, signs of the functions, related acute angles), exact values for 30°, 45° and 60° (π/6, π/4, π/3), and finding the other ratios from one given ratio and the quadrant.

concepts.name: Graphs of trigonometric functions
concepts.description: The graphs of sine, cosine and tangent over given domains in degrees or radians; amplitude and period; y = a sin bx + c, y = a cos bx + c and y = a tan bx + c (a a positive integer, b a simple fraction or integer, c an integer) with maximum and minimum values, intercepts and the asymptotes of tangent graphs labelled; finding a, b and c from a graph; using intersections to count solutions.

concepts.name: Trigonometric identities and proofs
concepts.description: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ, cot θ = cos θ / sin θ, sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ and cosec²θ = 1 + cot²θ; simplifying expressions and proving identities involving the six functions (working from one side, setting out a 'show that' clearly). Equations that need identities are in amath.trig.equations-identities.

concepts.name: Solving trigonometric equations
concepts.description: Solving equations such as sin x = k, cos x = k, tan x = k and their reciprocal forms in a given interval (degrees or radians): the principal value and the others from symmetry and period; equations in multiple or compound angles (sin 2x, cos(x/2 − π/3), cosec(2θ − π/2)); a sin x = b cos x via tan x; and products of factors equal to zero.

concepts.name: Trigonometric equations using identities
concepts.description: Equations that need an identity first, usually becoming a quadratic in one function (2 sin²x − cos x − 1 = 0, 2 sec²θ + tan θ − 3 = 0, 4 cot θ = tan θ), choosing the identity, rejecting impossible values (|sin x| ≤ 1, |sec x| ≥ 1), and checking that every solution in the interval has been found.

concepts.name: Permutations
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Factorial notation (0! = 1), the difference between permutations and combinations and when to use each, the formula for nPr, and arrangements of distinct objects in a line with conditions (particular items at the ends, items together or not together, forming numbers with given properties). Repeated objects, circular arrangements and problems needing both permutations and combinations are excluded.

concepts.name: Combinations
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The notation and formula for nCr, selections (committees, teams, choices from groups) with conditions (particular items included or excluded, at least or at most a number from a group) using the multiplication and addition principles, and algebraic problems such as solving nC2 = 45. Problems needing both permutations and combinations are excluded.

concepts.name: Sequences and their behaviour
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. A sequence as an ordered list of terms, notation u₁, u₂, …, uₙ, nth-term formulas and recurrence relations, and the behaviour of sequences: increasing, decreasing, periodic, oscillating, convergent (with its limit) and divergent, with examples of each.

concepts.name: Series and sigma notation
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. A series as the sum of the terms of a sequence, sigma (Σ) notation, writing a series in sigma notation and expanding a sum written in it, evaluating finite sums by listing or with the arithmetic and geometric series formulas, and simple properties such as Σ(aᵣ + bᵣ) = Σaᵣ + Σbᵣ and Σ c = nc.

concepts.name: Arithmetic progressions
concepts.description: Recognising an arithmetic progression and its common difference, the nth term a + (n − 1)d, the sum of the first n terms (both forms of the formula), finding a, d or n from given information (including the number of terms in a range, such as multiples of 7 between 100 and 300), and problems in context.

concepts.name: Geometric progressions
concepts.description: Recognising a geometric progression and its common ratio, telling geometric from arithmetic progressions, the nth term arⁿ⁻¹, the sum of the first n terms, finding n with logarithms, problems in context (growth, depreciation, compound interest), and problems combining an arithmetic and a geometric progression.

concepts.name: Convergent geometric progressions and the sum to infinity
concepts.description: The condition |r| < 1 for a geometric progression to converge, the sum to infinity a/(1 − r), explaining why a given progression has or does not have a sum to infinity, recurring decimals as geometric series, and problems such as the total distance travelled by a bouncing ball.

concepts.name: The binomial expansion
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Expanding (a + b)ⁿ for a positive integer n with binomial coefficients (nCr and Pascal's triangle), full expansions and the first few terms of expansions such as (2 − 3x)⁵ with simplified coefficients, and using an expansion to estimate a value (for example 1.02⁶).

concepts.name: Using the general term of a binomial expansion
concepts.description: Cambridge only. The general term nCr a^(n−r) b^r, finding a specified term or coefficient, the term independent of x in expansions such as (2x + 1/x)¹⁰, coefficients in products such as (1 + kx)(2 − x)⁶, and finding an unknown n or k from given coefficients. The greatest term and properties of the coefficients are excluded.

concepts.name: Vectors: notation, magnitude and unit vectors
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Vector notation (column vectors, AB with an arrow, bold letters, ai + bj), position vectors and AB = b − a, magnitude, unit vectors, adding and subtracting vectors and multiplying by scalars, parallel vectors, and finding unknowns by equating like vectors.

concepts.name: Vector geometry
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Expressing vectors in a figure in terms of given vectors, the position vector of a point dividing a line in a ratio, showing that points are collinear or that lines are parallel, and finding unknown scalars where two lines meet by equating the coefficients of non-parallel vectors.

concepts.name: Velocity vectors and relative position
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Composing and resolving velocities, speed as the magnitude of velocity, the position vector r = r₀ + tv of a particle moving with constant velocity, finding when particles collide or are a given distance apart, and resultant-velocity problems such as a boat crossing a river.

concepts.name: Gradients of curves and the derived function
concepts.description: The gradient of a curve at a point as the gradient of the tangent there, the informal idea of a limit through a sequence of chords (ZIMSEC asks for the gradient from first principles in simple cases; Cambridge needs only the informal idea), the derived function and the notations dy/dx, f′(x), d²y/dx², f″(x) and d/dx(…).

concepts.name: Differentiating powers of x
concepts.description: The derivative of xⁿ for any rational n, constant multiples, sums and differences, rewriting roots and reciprocals as powers before differentiating, evaluating a gradient at a point, and second derivatives.

concepts.name: The chain rule
concepts.description: Differentiating composite functions with the chain rule, especially powers of a function such as (3x² + 4)^(1/2) and (2 − 5x)⁻³, written in either notation (dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx). Exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric composites are practised in amath.calculus.trig-exp-log.

concepts.name: The product and quotient rules
concepts.description: Differentiating products uv and quotients u/v of functions (polynomials, powers, exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions), simplifying the result (factorising), and using it to find gradients.

concepts.name: Derivatives of trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions
concepts.description: The derivatives of sin x, cos x and tan x (x in radians), eˣ, ln x and 1/x, and of composites such as e^(3x−1), ln(2x + 5), sin 3x and cos²x by the chain rule, combined with the product and quotient rules.

concepts.name: Tangents and normals
concepts.description: Using differentiation to find the gradient at a point, the equations of the tangent and the normal to a curve at a point, points where the gradient takes a given value, where tangents or normals meet the axes or each other, and areas of the triangles they form.

concepts.name: Stationary points and their nature
concepts.description: Finding stationary points (dy/dx = 0), determining whether each is a maximum or a minimum with the first-derivative (change of sign) test and the second-derivative test, with full justification, and explaining how to tell a maximum from a minimum. Points of inflexion are excluded.

concepts.name: Practical maximum and minimum problems
concepts.description: Cambridge only (ZIMSEC applications name stationary points but not optimisation in context). Forming an expression for a quantity in one variable from a practical situation (boxes, cylinders, fencing, cost), using a constraint to eliminate a variable, finding the stationary value, justifying that it is a maximum or minimum, and answering in context.

concepts.name: Rates of change and connected rates of change
concepts.description: The derivative as a rate of change, and connected rates of change with the chain rule (dy/dt = dy/dx × dx/dt), for example the rate of increase of the area of a circle or of the volume of a sphere or cone, or the rate at which a liquid level rises.

concepts.name: Small increments and approximations
concepts.description: The approximation δy ≈ (dy/dx) δx for small changes, approximate changes and percentage changes in a quantity (for example the area of a square or the volume of a sphere), and approximate values of functions near a known value.

concepts.name: Integration as the reverse of differentiation
concepts.description: Integration as the reverse process of differentiation, notation ∫ … dx, the arbitrary constant, integrating sums of powers of x (n ≠ −1, including roots and reciprocals rewritten as powers), finding the equation of a curve from its gradient function and a point, and 'hence' integrals that use a derivative found earlier.

concepts.name: Integrating exponential, trigonometric and linear-composite functions
concepts.description: Integrating (ax + b)ⁿ for any rational n including n = −1 (giving (1/a) ln(ax + b)), 1/x, e^(ax+b), sin(ax + b), cos(ax + b) and (Cambridge) sec²(ax + b), with angles in radians and the arbitrary constant.

concepts.name: Definite integrals and plane areas
concepts.description: Evaluating definite integrals, the area between a curve and the x-axis (including regions below the axis), the area between a line and a curve, between two curves, and areas made of two parts.

concepts.name: Volumes of revolution
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The volume generated when the region under y = f(x) between x = a and x = b is rotated through 360° about the x-axis, V = π∫y² dx, for simple polynomial, root and exponential functions, with exact answers in terms of π. Rotation about the y-axis is excluded (to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus).

concepts.name: Kinematics with calculus
concepts.description: Cambridge only. Displacement, velocity and acceleration of a particle moving in a straight line with variable or constant acceleration: v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt, integrating back with initial conditions, instantaneous rest and change of direction, distance travelled versus displacement, and displacement–time, distance–time, velocity–time, speed–time and acceleration–time graphs. Constant-acceleration (suvat) mechanics for ZIMSEC is in amath.mechanics.constant-acceleration.

concepts.name: Probability language: sample spaces, events and Venn diagrams
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Trials, sample spaces, outcomes and events, equally likely outcomes, set notation for events (A ∪ B, A ∩ B, A′), illustrating two or three events on Venn diagrams and finding probabilities from them.

concepts.name: Approaches to probability
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Objective probability, both classical (theoretical, from equally likely outcomes) and experimental (relative frequency in the long run), and subjective probability (a degree of belief); comparing the approaches, the probability scale, and expected frequencies.

concepts.name: Addition and product rules, outcome tables and tree diagrams
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Mutually exclusive events and the addition rule P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B), the general rule P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), independent events and the product rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), outcome (possibility) tables and tree diagrams with and without replacement.

concepts.name: Conditional probability
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) from tables, Venn diagrams and tree diagrams, testing independence (P(A | B) = P(A)), and finding a 'reverse' conditional probability from a tree diagram.

concepts.name: Statistical terms, sources and types of data
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Key terms (statistics, data, frequency, tally, population, sample, census), primary and secondary data and their sources with merits and demerits, classifying data, and qualitative versus quantitative and discrete versus continuous data.

concepts.name: Collecting, organising and presenting data
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Methods of collecting data (questionnaires, interviews, observation, experiments, records) with merits and demerits, tally charts and frequency tables, grouped frequency tables (class limits, boundaries, widths and midpoints), and presenting data in bar charts, pie charts, histograms (including unequal class widths and frequency density), frequency polygons, cumulative frequency curves and stem-and-leaf diagrams, choosing an appropriate form.

concepts.name: Mean, median and mode
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The mean, median and mode of raw data, ungrouped frequency distributions and grouped data (estimated mean from midpoints, median by interpolation or from a cumulative frequency curve, modal class), the relationship between mean, median and mode for symmetric and skewed data, and choosing an appropriate average.

concepts.name: Measures of dispersion
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Range, quartiles and interquartile range, variance and standard deviation of raw, frequency and grouped data (Σ(x − x̄)²/n and Σx²/n − x̄²), the coefficient of variation (σ/x̄ × 100%), why measures of dispersion matter, and comparing distributions.

concepts.name: Discrete random variables
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Discrete random variables and their probability distributions (tables, ΣP = 1), finding unknown probabilities, the expectation E(X) = Σxp and the variance Var(X) = Σx²p − [E(X)]², and cumulative probabilities.

concepts.name: The binomial distribution
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The conditions for a binomial model, X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = nCr pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ, cumulative probabilities (at most, at least, between), the mean np and variance np(1 − p), finding n or p from given information, and modelling in context.

concepts.name: Continuous random variables
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Continuous random variables and probability density functions (f(x) ≥ 0, total area 1), finding an unknown constant, probabilities as areas P(a < X < b) = ∫f(x) dx, P(X = a) = 0, and E(X) = ∫x f(x) dx and Var(X) = ∫x² f(x) dx − [E(X)]² for simple polynomial pdfs.

concepts.name: The normal distribution
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The properties of the normal curve (bell-shaped, symmetric about μ, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations), X ~ N(μ, σ²), standardising Z = (X − μ)/σ, using standard normal tables Φ(z) for probabilities to the left, right and between values, and the reverse use of the tables to find z, then x, from a probability.

concepts.name: Finding the mean or standard deviation of a normal distribution
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Finding an unknown mean μ or standard deviation σ, or both (simultaneous equations), of a normal distribution from given probabilities, using the inverse normal tables, in context.

concepts.name: Populations, samples and sampling methods
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Population, sample, sampling frame, census versus sample survey and reasons for sampling; random sampling (simple random using lots or random numbers, systematic, stratified, cluster) and non-random sampling (quota, convenience); bias, representative samples, and the advantages and disadvantages of each method.

concepts.name: The distribution of the sample mean and the central limit theorem
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The sample mean X̄ as a random variable, E(X̄) = μ and Var(X̄) = σ²/n, X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) when X is normal, the central limit theorem (used without proof) for large samples from any population, and probabilities about a sample mean.

concepts.name: Point estimates: unbiased estimators of the mean and variance
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Estimators and estimates, unbiased estimates of the population mean (x̄) and variance (s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1), equivalently n/(n − 1) times the sample variance) from raw data and from summary statistics Σx and Σx², and the standard error of the mean σ/√n.

concepts.name: Confidence intervals for a population mean
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Interval estimates, confidence intervals x̄ ± z σ/√n for the mean of a normal population with known variance, or of any population from a large sample (σ estimated by s), at the 95% and 99% levels (5% and 1% significance), interpretation, the margin of error, and the sample size needed for a given width.

concepts.name: Displacement, velocity and acceleration; motion graphs
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Scalars and vectors (distance and displacement, speed and velocity), average speed, displacement–time graphs (gradient = velocity), velocity–time graphs (gradient = acceleration, area = displacement), and sketching and interpreting multi-stage journeys. Calculus kinematics (Cambridge) is in amath.calculus.kinematics.

concepts.name: Equations of motion for constant acceleration
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The equations v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, s = ½(u + v)t and s = vt − ½at², sign conventions, vertical motion under gravity (g stated in the question), and two-particle problems (meeting and overtaking).

concepts.name: Forces as vectors: resultants and components
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Force and its unit, types of force (weight, normal reaction, tension, thrust, friction, applied forces), representing forces as vectors (components or magnitude and direction), the resultant of two or more forces by components or by the triangle and cosine rule, and resolving a force into perpendicular components.

concepts.name: Equilibrium of a particle
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of the forces on it is zero; resolving in two perpendicular directions, three forces in equilibrium (triangle of forces), particles hanging on strings and resting on smooth inclined planes, and finding unknown forces and angles.

concepts.name: Friction
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. The contact force between two surfaces as a normal reaction and a frictional force, F ≤ μR, limiting equilibrium and the coefficient of friction, smooth and rough surfaces, and particles in equilibrium on rough horizontal and inclined planes. Friction during motion is in amath.mechanics.newtons-laws-planes.

concepts.name: Newton's laws of motion
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Newton's three laws, F = ma for a particle of constant mass under constant forces, weight W = mg, horizontal and vertical motion (including lifts and objects moving against resistance), combined with the equations of motion.

concepts.name: Newton's second law with resolved forces and friction
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Applying F = ma when forces act at an angle or on inclined planes, on smooth and rough surfaces (F = μR while sliding), finding accelerations, forces and coefficients of friction, combined with the equations of motion. Connected particles over pulleys are not named in the syllabus and are excluded.

concepts.name: Work, kinetic energy and potential energy
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Work done by a constant force when its point of application moves (Fd, and Fd cos θ for a force at an angle), kinetic energy ½mv², gravitational potential energy mgh, the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, and the work–energy principle with work done against resistance, on slopes and in vertical motion.

concepts.name: Power
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only. Power as the rate of doing work, P = W/t, P = Fv for a vehicle moving at speed v with driving force F, the watt and kilowatt, maximum speed when the driving force equals the resistance, and acceleration at a given speed using F = ma.
